images.caption: Marine chronometer (1948) displaying its second hand advancing in half-second increments over a sub-dial marked with 60 seconds, for optimal timing of angle measurements celestial objects. The timepiece is technically based on the German Einheitschronometer developed during World War II and was made by A. Lange & Söhne in Glashütte bei Dresden (Glashütte near Dresden). Roman numerals mark the hours on the dail instead of Arabic numerals used on the Einheitschronometer dail. The production of German unified-design chronometers, with their harmonized components, continued until long after World War II in Germany and the Soviet Union, who confiscated the original Einheitschronometer technical drawings and set up a production line in Moscow in 1949.[1] The German Einheitschronometer ultimately became the mechanical marine timekeeper design produced in the highest volume, with about 58,000 units produced. Of these, fewer than 3,000 were produced during World War II, about 5,000 after the war in West and East Germany and about 50,000 in the Soviet Union and later post-Soviet Russia.
